analysis.one_liner: Imposes a 0.03% tax on stock, bond, and derivative trades to curb speculation.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a hearing or a vote in the House Ways and Means Committee and died when the 113th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would add a tax of 0.03% — three cents per $100 — on purchases of stocks, bonds, derivatives, and similar financial instruments traded in the U.S. or by U.S. parties [S2][S3]. The tax is aimed at high-volume speculative trading; initial stock and bond offerings and short-term debt (100 days or less) are exempt, and savers get a tax credit refunding the tax on money put into retirement accounts, health savings accounts, and college savings plans [S2][S3]. The revenue would go to the general Treasury; the bill does not dedicate it to any specific program.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary savers and long-term investors, who are protected by the credit that refunds the tax on contributions to 401(k)s, IRAs, health savings accounts, and college savings plans [S3]. Taxpayers generally benefit if the revenue offsets other taxes or funds public priorities, though the bill leaves that choice to future Congresses. The tax is also designed to discourage rapid-fire speculative trading that adds costs and instability to markets.

how_it_helps.text: It taxes the volume of financial trading rather than wages or purchases, so a retiree moving money between funds pays pennies while a high-frequency firm executing millions of trades pays a real bill.

It fully offsets the tax on contributions to tax-exempt retirement plans, health savings accounts, Archer MSAs, 529 college plans, and Coverdell accounts, so everyday saving through those vehicles is not penalized.

It reaches transactions routed offshore, applying the tax when any party is a U.S. person and treating controlled foreign corporations of U.S. owners as U.S. persons, to keep traders from simply moving the activity abroad.
It exempts initial issuances of stocks and bonds, so companies raising capital for investment do not pay the tax — only secondary-market trading is taxed.

analysis.who_pays: Financial trading firms, including high-frequency traders, hedge funds, banks, and brokers, bear the tax directly — trading facilities and brokers collect it on transactions they clear or execute [S3]. Some of the cost could be passed to everyday investors through wider bid-ask spreads or higher fund trading costs, though the offset for tax-favored accounts shields most retirement and education saving [S3]. Traders might also shift some activity to foreign markets to avoid the tax.
analysis.who_pays_short: Wall Street trading firms and speculators

drawbacks.text: The revenue is not dedicated to anything — it flows to the general Treasury, so the bill does not itself fund student aid, infrastructure, or any other specific public purpose despite the broad set of policy subjects attached to it.

Trading taxes tend to widen trading costs, and some of the burden can land on ordinary investors through fund expense ratios and spreads, even with the credit for tax-favored accounts covering contributions rather than all trading inside those accounts.

Requiring the tax on any transaction involving a U.S. party could push some trading to foreign venues and reduce U.S. market volume, an outcome critics of transaction taxes have long argued raises costs for everyone.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The design is unusually careful for a transaction tax: it exempts new issuances and short-term debt, credits the tax back for retirement, health, and education savings, and tries to catch transactions routed through foreign entities. The main honest objections are that the revenue is unearmarked and that a small residual cost could reach ordinary investors through trading spreads. On balance the burden falls on high-volume trading, which is the stated point of the bill.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the Ways and Means Committee the day it was introduced, never got a hearing or a vote, and died when the 113th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Peter DeFazio introduced the Wall Street Trading and Speculators Tax Act on February 28, 2013, with 20 original cosponsors, all Democrats.
The bill was referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means the same day, and no further action was ever taken on it.
It accumulated 27 cosponsors over the two-year Congress, every one of them a Democrat, and never reached the House floor.
The Congress ended on January 3, 2015, and the bill expired without a vote.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Financial trading firms — banks, hedge funds, and high-frequency traders — are better off because the bill never advanced, since they avoided a new tax on every trade. The committee leadership that never scheduled action also kept a tax off the books that would have been difficult to repeal later.

for.name: Rep. Peter DeFazio
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited 20 original cosponsors on the day of introduction.

for.name: 27 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; no Republican ever did.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee leadership
against.role: Committee of referral (Chair Rep. Dave Camp, R-MI)
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or markup on the bill after its referral; it sat without action for the rest of the Congress.

against.name: Wall Street trading firms and financial trade groups
against.what_they_did: Opposed transaction taxes on securities and derivatives trading during this period, as they had in prior Congresses.

sides.party_line_note: All 27 cosponsors were House Democrats and the committee that received the bill was controlled by Republicans, so the split ran entirely along party lines — though no vote ever occurred to measure it.

industries.note: The tax scales with trading volume, so firms executing huge numbers of rapid trades would pay the most; their profit model depends on exactly the activity the bill is designed to discourage. Its defeat left their revenue untouched.

They would pay 0.03% on purchases of stocks, bonds, derivatives, and notional principal contracts, including deals involving their offshore affiliates. Avoiding the tax preserves a revenue stream that ordinary taxpayers do not share in.

Trading facilities and U.S. brokers are legally responsible for collecting and remitting the tax on transactions they clear or execute, adding compliance and administrative costs. Killing the bill spared them that burden.

industries.industry: Mutual funds and retirement plan managers
industries.note: Their funds trade taxable securities, but the bill credits the tax back on contributions to the retirement and college savings accounts they administer, softening the effect on their core savers. Their interest in this bill largely runs alongside savers' interests.
